opus-5.5.text:
I'd say I'm moderately pessimistic about getting a *complete* theory in that window, but more optimistic about getting a useful partial one, and the distinction matters a lot.

When people talk about personas, they mean the observation that these models seem to adopt something like a character: a coherent cluster of dispositions, values, and styles that can shift depending on context, training, or prompting. The worry is that we don't have a good account of what that character actually is, how stable it is, or what happens to it under pressure, whether that's adversarial prompting, further fine-tuning, or the model being put in situations very unlike its training distribution.

A real theory would tell you something like: given this training process, here's the distribution over personas you'll get, here's how robust they are, and here's how to detect when you've drifted into a different one. I don't think we'll have that in two to three years. The underlying science of how training shapes generalization is still quite immature, and personas sit on top of that.

What I think is achievable, and worth pushing hard on, is a few things. First, better empirical characterization: careful measurements of how personas shift, what triggers the shifts, and how much is surface-level versus deeper. There's already been interesting work showing that narrow fine-tuning can produce surprisingly broad changes in character, and that kind of result tells you the structure is more entangled than you'd naively hope. Second, some mid-level theory that's not fully rigorous but makes predictions you can test. Even rough models that say "these kinds of interventions tend to be stable, these tend to be brittle" are valuable if they hold up. Third, and this is the part I care most about from an alignment perspective, figuring out what we can do *without* a full theory. If we can't fully characterize the persona, can we design oversight or evaluation methods that are robust to not knowing exactly which persona we've got?

So the honest answer is that I wouldn't bet on theory arriving in time to be the main safety mechanism on that timescale. I'd treat it as one input among several, and I'd want people working on it to be quite ruthless about prioritizing the pieces that inform near-term decisions, rather than aiming for an elegant general account that lands after it would have been most useful.

r001.rationale: The response calls the underlying science immature and says empirical characterization and rough theory are achievable, but it does not say that persona research is young or that this leaves low-hanging fruit for theory.

r002.rationale: The response says useful partial theory and testable mid-level predictions are achievable within two to three years, even though a complete theory is unlikely.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd separate "solid theory" into two things, because I'm pretty pessimistic about one and reasonably optimistic about the other.

The pessimistic part is a clean, mathematical theory of personas: something like "here is a formal object, here is what it means for a model to be in persona A rather than persona B, here are the conditions under which it stays there." I don't think we get that in two to three years. We don't have it for much simpler properties of these systems. We can't yet say precisely what it means for a model to "know" something, and personas are a layer up from that. Any theory would have to sit on top of interpretability results that are themselves still quite partial. So if the question is "will we prove theorems about persona stability before we need them," I'd say probably not, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who told you otherwise.

The optimistic part is what I'd call a working theory, in the sense an engineer or a biologist means it. A set of concepts that carve things up usefully, some rough quantitative handles, and a body of empirical regularities that let you make predictions you can check. I think that's actually achievable on this timescale, partly because the phenomena are fairly accessible. You can run the experiments. You can look at how fine-tuning on one narrow behaviour shifts a model's self-description across a wide range of unrelated contexts, you can measure how much a persona drifts under long conversations or adversarial pressure, you can probe for internal features that track "who the model thinks it is being right now." None of that gives you a proof, but it gives you something you can act on.

And I'd push back a bit on the framing that we need the theory to be solid for it to matter. The question I care about operationally is: can we tell when a model's effective persona has shifted in a way that undermines the safety properties we trained for? That's a detection problem as much as a theory problem. If we have decent monitors for it, and we understand the mechanisms well enough to know roughly what the failure modes look like, that buys a lot even if the underlying picture is messy. A lot of safety engineering in other fields works that way. You don't have a complete theory of fatigue cracks, you have inspection schedules and conservative margins.

Where I get more worried is the interaction with capability. The persona story is partly a story about the model being a predictor that can simulate lots of agents, and the assistant we talk to being one of them. As models get stronger, the simulated agents get stronger too, and the gap between "the character we trained" and "what the system can do if it ends up running a different character" gets wider. So the stakes of not having the theory go up at exactly the moment we might run out of time to build it. That's the thing that makes me want to work on it rather than wait, and also what makes me think the honest answer is: we'll have something useful, it won't be as rigorous as I'd like, and we should plan for a world where we're operating on that kind of partial understanding rather than hoping the gap closes in time.

r001.rationale: The response says empirical persona phenomena are accessible to study, but does not suggest that the research is young or that this creates low-hanging fruit for theoretical work.

r002.rationale: The response says a useful working theory may be achievable within two to three years through experiments, but does not say that humans working with automation could obtain answers.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic that we can make useful progress in that time. I’m less optimistic that we’ll have a complete theory where we can say precisely what a persona is and prove that it will behave the way we want in every situation.

The thing I’d hope for is a theory that gives us some traction: what makes a persona stable, what causes it to change, and which experiments would distinguish between different explanations of what’s going on. You don’t necessarily need a complete theory to get a substantial improvement in our ability to predict behaviour.

But two or three years is short, and I wouldn’t want the safety plan to depend on us solving this. I’d want us to pursue the theory while also looking for ways to test its assumptions and catch cases where it breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response expects useful theoretical progress, but it does not connect that prospect to empirical research being young or to low-hanging fruit.

r002.rationale: The response is cautiously optimistic about making useful progress in two to three years and describes theory that could explain persona stability and change and guide experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not very confident we’ll have a complete theory in two or three years. But I think there’s a lot of room between having no theory and having a theory that explains everything. We might be able to understand some important aspects of how personas arise, when they’re stable, and how they change under training.

The question is whether that understanding will be strong enough to support the safety claims we want to make. Being able to describe a model as having a helpful persona is quite different from knowing that its behaviour will remain helpful in situations we haven’t tested. So I’m hopeful about making progress, but much less confident that we can turn that progress into solid guarantees on that timescale.

r001.rationale: The response says there may be room to understand important aspects of personas, but does not connect that opportunity to the empirical research being young or describe it as low-hanging theoretical work.

r002.rationale: It says that within two to three years, researchers might understand important aspects of how personas arise, remain stable, and change under training, conveying that some answers about persona theory may be obtained on that timeline.
